newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's Arthuis irked by Juppe policy grip-radio.
newsitem.headline: France's Arthuis irked by Juppe policy grip-radio.

text.p: French Finance Minister Jean Arthuis had to be talked out of resigning over Prime Minister Alain Juppe's insistence on controlling economic policy himself, a veteran political commentator said on Friday.

"Jean Arthuis is very unhappy to see his real responsibilities taken over by Alain Juppe. It is the prime minister alone who announces the major budgetary and fiscal decisions," RTL radio commentator Philippe Alexandre said.
"Jean Arthuis has the feeling of being a minister who is mute, in other words non-existent," he said.
Arthuis felt he would be better off back at the Senate, the upper house of parliament, and talked often about resigning.

"These last few days it took all the eloquence and charm of (President) Jacques Chirac himself and (Senate head) Rene Monory, his protector and mentor, to talk him out of slamming the door behind him," Alexandre said.

Juppe, himself a former budget minister, has kept an unusually tight grip on economic policy since he took office last May. He forced his first finance minister, Alain Madelin, to resign last August after less than three months in office and has left little for Arthuis to handle.
Orthodox fiscal proposals drawn up by the finance ministry have often appeared to be discarded for political reasons by a prime minister with an eye to 1998 parliamentary elections.

For example, a detailed report the finance ministry drew up in May said there was no room for tax cuts next year given the need to reduce the budget deficit. Juppe last week announced income tax cuts of 25 billion francs ($4.84 billion).

In the most recent case, Juppe promised to base a parliamentary debate on the introduction of pension funds on a draft bill drawn up by three members of parliament rather than on detailed proposals put forward by Arthuis.

After the prime minister fired Madelin last year, official sources suggested the row between the two men was mainly over Madelin's outspoken approach to policies which Juppe preferred to try to carry out more quietly.
Arthuis has been careful not to rock the boat, avoiding speaking publicly about anything controversial.
On the one occasion when he did float a sensitive proposal aloud -- phasing out the 20 percent income tax deduction for salaried workers -- Juppe promptly disowned him.
While there have been sporadic rumours in financial markets that Arthuis may be ready to quit, the government is seen as unwilling to lose two finance ministers in a row. ($1=5.163 French Franc)
